idiom_name: Data.define immutable value snapshots + Array#bsearch_index over effective dates
implementation_notes: Data.define (Ruby 3.2) gives the version role without boilerplate: instances expose no writers and #with returns a changed copy, so publishing is exactly copy the current version, then add the copy. The continuity is an ordinary object holding an array of versions ordered by an effective Date, and the as-of lookup is Array#bsearch_index with a find-minimum block (first entry whose effective date is after the query), minus one for the version in force - bsearch_index is stdlib, so no scan or index array is needed. Older code bases use frozen Struct instances with the same bsearch block; no gem is required.
code_sketch:
Version = Data.define(:effective, :terms)            # immutable snapshot (Ruby 3.2)
class Contract                                       # continuity, history ascending by effective
  def as_of(on)
    i = @history.bsearch_index { |v| v.effective > on } || @history.size
    i.zero? ? nil : @history[i - 1]                  # nil = Missing Version
  end
  def current = @history.last
  def amend(effective, working)                      # working = current.with(terms: ...)
    at = @history.bsearch_index { |v| v.effective > effective } || @history.size
    @history.insert(at, Version.new(effective:, terms: working.terms))
  end
end
pitfalls: Data values are shallowly immutable: a mutable member (Array, Hash, String used as a buffer) can still be changed through its own methods - Data does no deep-freeze, so freeze or copy the payload when publishing.
Array#bsearch needs a monotone block (all false, then all true) over a sorted array and returns nil for a non-monotone block instead of raising, so amend must keep the array ordered.
Ruby Date and Time are different classes and comparing them raises, and ActiveSupport's TimeWithZone adds a third - pick Date or Time consistently for effective dates.
bsearch_index with a find-any block returns an arbitrary matching index; the find-minimum form (single comparison per element) is the one that implements a boundary lookup.
